summary:
Finding optimal routes and parking spaces on Mars is a difficult task that involves avoiding uneven terrain, finding the flattest paths, and staying in sections with the most sunlight for both heat and energy. So, we created MarMap, a comprehensive map of the Martian land that can determine and visualize an optimal path for a rover carrying a crew of astronauts on a Mars walk. By putting together elevation, thermal inertia, and shade data together, we’re able calculate the best path from Point A to Point B. We target surfaces that have high thermal inertia which are harder, areas with low shade to maximize time spent in the sun for powering photovoltaic devices, and routes that are the flattest possible for easy travel. 

In the future, when traveling to Mars becomes feasible, we need astronauts to embark on walks that can reveal our Martian neighbor’s history. These walks are dangerous especially in such uncharted territory and knowing what route and parking spot is best is crucial for optimizing power and having a successful science walk. Every last bit of power and time is important for science and without MarMap, science can very quickly become lost.
details:
MarMap takes real data from JPL and uses it as a series of weights before considering the most optimal path. We first took elevation data from JPL and turned it into a readable format, organizing the data into a grid pattern with spatial resolution being 20m per pixel. We specifically targeted Gale Crater as a demo site for our product due to it having more precise data with much clearer resolution. We then decided to move on to figuring out a basic pathfinding algorithm just for the elevation data, taking into consideration the slope between the targeted tile and its neighboring tiles. After some basic research, we decided that a 15 degree maximum slope would be added so that if any slope is above 15 degrees, it would avoid that tile in favor of something more flat. Say if the target is on top of a mountain, our idea was that the pathfinding would travel as far up as possible with the 15 degree limit until it couldn’t. That’s where it would mark the parking spot. Our initial approach was to use Dijkstra’s Algorithm but we realized that its method of search branches out radially, searching much more tiles than needed. So we pivoted to an A* algorithm approach where the search is guided toward the target instead of spreading out in every direction. Each tile is scored by the distance already traveled plus an estimate of the distance remaining. A* helped us handle much larger areas, and when the target can’t be reached under the 15° limit, the search stops at the reachable tile closest to the target, which becomes the parking spot, later on factoring other layers like shade level and solidity of the surface.

After implementing the pathfinding algorithm, we moved onto adding even more layers of data that would change up the weights for each edge. We started off with shade data calculated by taking a point in the sky at a certain sun angle (azimuth) and then shooting a raycast from that point to a target tile. If that raycast were to hit any elevated tile before the target tile, then it would add a shade value to that tile. Another layer of data was added in the form of thermal inertia data, downloaded and then matched up via the local coordinates of both the elevation data and the thermal inertia data. Again, we added more weight calculations to paths by favoring tiles with high thermal inertia as that indicated that the material was more solid and therefore safer. We used matplotlib and python to test out the backend of our project and once it was all good, we were finally able to start working on the frontend and connecting the two parts of our project.

Frontend wise, we used React, taking a chunk of optical data that had the same coordinates around Gale Crater. Using Three.js, we were able to get a scrollable 2D and 3D view of the map with relevant layers that accompanied the project such as the thermal inertia map, shade map, and elevation map. The idea was to take the coordinate of the click and pass that through the API to the backend for calculations to be done and then fetch that data back onto the frontend in order for the user to be able to see the path. Using the same backend logic written in python, we attached that to the API and was able to get basic communication between the two parts. Numba was used to speed up calculations on the backend. Furthermore, on paths that were separated by a large distance, we sped up calculations by lowering the spatial resolution a little from 20m to 40m or more in order for less tiles to be computed. For shorter paths the same 20m resolution was used. 

In terms of the idea, we thought it was pretty cool to implement Google Maps onto Mars. Except Mars is much more unfriendly than Earth. Sure, on Earth you might take 20 laps around the same 3 blocks trying to find parking in a busy city, but at least the fear of your car falling through soft surfaces or coming back to a dead car isn’t there. Instead of usual pathfinding weights, we incorporated all kinds of data ranging from elevation to surface hardness in order to achieve the best possible route. With MarMap, navigating Mars will feel a lot safer than driving on unpaved roads where the whole planet seems to find ways to screw you over.
